title: Early Adopters: Navigating AI Integration in Special Education Teacher Preparation
extended_summary:
This article addresses how generative AI can be integrated into special education teacher preparation in ways that are practical, ethical, and instructionally useful. The authors argue that AI is reshaping teaching and learning, and they position AI as a tool that can support curriculum alignment, assignment design, lesson and case study generation, assessment development, and reflective coaching.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it is a practice-based and reflective conceptual piece grounded in the authors’ experiences as faculty and administrators in teacher preparation programs at two universities in the Northeastern United States. The context includes undergraduate and graduate teacher preparation courses serving both special education and general education candidates, with a particular emphasis on pre-service special educators. Examples include using chatbots for prompt engineering, lesson planning, differentiated supports for learners with disabilities and emergent bilinguals, video-based coaching, and AI-supported formative assessment tools.

The authors conclude that AI can enhance efficiency and personalization in teacher preparation, but only when it is used critically and with strong attention to ethics, bias, transparency, and human judgment. They emphasize that AI-generated outputs should be treated as starting points rather than final products, and that faculty expertise remains essential for contextualizing instructional decisions, especially in special education settings. The article also highlights the need for future research on AI’s impact on educator preparation and student learning outcomes.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/practice-oriented article with no clear empirical study design, no comparison group, and no reported quantitative outcomes. It is peer-reviewed, but it is not intervention research and provides primarily descriptive examples and professional recommendations.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measurable impacts or effect sizes on learner or teacher outcomes. Its contribution is conceptual and descriptive rather than evidence of demonstrated impact.

interventions.use_case: generative AI chatbots and LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) used by teacher educators and teacher candidates to draft and refine course outcomes, lesson plans, case studies, prompts, and reflective coaching questions in special education teacher preparation

AI-assisted feedback/coaching tools for teacher reflection and assessment, including video-based coaching (e.g., Vosaic AI Mate) and instructional writing/discussion support (e.g., Packback) that generate time-stamped feedback, prompts, and performance annotations

AI-supported writing and language assistance for drafting rubrics, lesson objectives, assessments, and student writing/discussion scaffolds, including support for prompt engineering and revision of AI-generated text

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that generative AI substantially reduced faculty time spent on curriculum alignment, syllabus/lesson drafting, rubric creation, and feedback generation in special education teacher preparation. No quantitative effect size is reported, but the authors repeatedly describe substantial time savings and offloading of lower-order tasks (e.g., course design, prompt-based revision, video annotation) that allowed more time for higher-level instructional work.
finding.measure: Perceived faculty workload/time savings and efficiency in curriculum design, lesson development, and feedback/coaching

finding.finding_summary: AI-supported tools such as Packback, Vosaic AI Mate, and Otter.ai are presented as ways to scale feedback, annotation, transcription, and assessment analysis. The paper does not report experimental data, but it clearly claims these tools reduce instructor workload and increase efficiency in providing real-time or time-stamped coaching, discourse support, and qualitative data analysis.
finding.measure: Faculty and teacher-candidate workload reduction; speed of annotation, transcription, and feedback generation

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes improved prompt engineering, critical evaluation of AI outputs, reflective practice, and pedagogical documentation as key skills developed through AI use. Although no quantitative outcomes are reported, the authors describe teacher candidates becoming more sophisticated at crafting contextualized prompts and using AI to support analysis, reflection, and revision.
finding.measure: Prompt quality, reflective ability, and critical analysis of AI outputs

finding.finding_summary: The paper is primarily a conceptual/practice article arguing that AI adoption can reshape special education teacher preparation, assessment norms, and ethical protocols. The authors highlight institutional needs for transparent AI policies, consent procedures, bias mitigation, and shifts toward pedagogical documentation, but they do not provide outcome data.
finding.measure: Institutional policy, ethical norms, and teacher-preparation practice change
